The Father's witness is given <reference osisRef="Heb.5.10">He 5:10</reference>. The Son's, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5">He 10:5</reference>. Now is added that of the Holy Spirit, called accordingly "the Spirit of grace," <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">He 10:29</reference>. The testimony of all Three leads to the same conclusion (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.18">He 10:18</reference>).<div eID="gen38921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for after that he had said before--</hi>The conclusion to the sentence is in <reference osisRef="Heb.10.17">He 10:17</reference>, "After He had said before, This is the covenant that I will make with them (with the house of Israel, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">He 8:10</reference>; here extended to the spiritual Israel) ... saith the Lord; I will put (literally, 'giving,' referring to the giving of the law; not now as then, giving into the hands, but giving) My laws into their hearts ('mind,' <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">He 8:10</reference>) and in their minds ('hearts,' <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">He 8:10</reference>); I will inscribe (so the Greek) them (here He omits the addition quoted in <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">He 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.11">11</reference>, I will be to them a God ... and they shall not teach every man his neighbor ...), and (that is, after He had said the foregoing, He then adds) their sins ... will I remember no more." The great object of the quotation here is to prove that, there being in the Gospel covenant, "REMISSION of sins" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.17">He 10:17</reference>), there is no more need of a sacrifice for sins. The object of the same quotation in <reference osisRef="Heb.8.8-Heb.8.13">He 8:8-13</reference> is to show that, there being a "NEW covenant," the old is antiquated. <div eID="gen38922" type="x-p"/>
entries.135bf2d4c3bd654db5db659eaa086f845256f7dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18504"/><div sID="gen38923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18504"/><hi type="bold">18. where remission of these is--</hi>as there is under the Gospel covenant (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.17">He 10:17</reference>). "Here ends the finale (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.18">He 10:1-18</reference>) of the great tripartite arrangement (He 7:1-25; 7:26-9:12; 9:13-10:18) of the middle portion of the Epistle. Its great theme was Christ a High Priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec. What it is to be a high priest after the order of Melchisedec is set forth, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1-Heb.7.25">He 7:1-25</reference>, as contrasted with the Aaronic order. That Christ, however, as High Priest, is Aaron's antitype in the true holy place, by virtue of His self-sacrifice here on earth, and Mediator of a better covenant, whose essential character the old only typified, we learn, He 7:26-9:12. And that Christ's self-sacrifice, offered through the Eternal Spirit, is of everlasting power, as contrasted with the unavailing cycle of legal offerings, is established in the third part, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13-Heb.10.18">He 9:13-10:18</reference>; the first half of this last portion [He 9:13-28], showing that both our present possession of salvation, and our future completion of it, are as certain to us as that He is with God, ruling as a Priest and reigning as a King, once more to appear, no more as a bearer of our sins, but in glory as a Judge. The second half, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.18">He 10:1-18</reference>, reiterating the main position of the whole, the High Priesthood of Christ, grounded on His offering of Himself--its kingly character its eternal accomplishment of its end, confirmed by Psalms 40 and 110 and Jeremiah 31" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <div eID="gen38923" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6176c91b0234e067852bb9d2fd848b67e8075f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18505"/><div sID="gen38924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18505"/>19. Here begins the third and last division of the Epistle; our duty now while waiting for the Lord's second advent. Resumption and expansion of the exhortation (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.14-Heb.4.16">He 4:14-16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">He 10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">23</reference> here) wherewith he closed the first part of the Epistle, preparatory to his great doctrinal argument, beginning at <reference osisRef="Heb.7.1">He 7:1</reference>.<div eID="gen38924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boldness--</hi>"free confidence," grounded on the consciousness that our sins have been forgiven.<div eID="gen38925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to enter--</hi>literally, "as regards the entering."<div eID="gen38926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by--</hi>Greek, "in"; it is in the blood of Jesus that our boldness to enter is grounded. Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.3.12">Ep 3:12</reference>, "In whom we have boldness and access with confidence." It is His having once for all entered as our Forerunner (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.20">He 6:20</reference>) and High Priest (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.21">He 10:21</reference>), making atonement for us with His blood, which is continually there (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">He 12:24</reference>) before God, that gives us confident access. No priestly caste now mediates between the sinner and his Judge. We may come boldly with loving confidence, not with slavish fear, directly through Christ, the only mediating Priest. The minister is not officially nearer God than the layman; nor can the latter serve God at a distance or by deputy, as the natural man would like. Each must come for himself, and all are accepted when they come by the new and living way opened by Christ. Thus all Christians are, in respect to access directly to God, virtually high priests (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>). They draw nigh in and through Christ, the only proper High Priest (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.25">He 7:25</reference>). <div eID="gen38927" type="x-p"/>
entries.760f793dfff363578c4bfd7149138458c96e90d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18506"/><div sID="gen38928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18506"/><hi type="bold">20. which, &c.--</hi>The antecedent in the Greek is "the entering"; not as English Version, "way." Translate, "which (entering) He has consecrated (not as though it were already existing, but has been the first to open, INAUGURATED as a new thing; see on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.18">He 9:18</reference>, where the Greek is the same) for us (as) a new (Greek, 'recent'; recently opened, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Ro 16:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.26">26</reference>) and living way" (not like the lifeless way through the law offering of the blood of dead victims, but real, vital, and of perpetual efficacy, because the living and life-giving Saviour is that way. It is a living hope that we have, producing not dead, but living, works). Christ, the first-fruits of our nature, has ascended, and the rest is sanctified thereby. "Christ's ascension is our promotion; and whither the glory of the Head hath preceded, thither the hope of the body, too, is called" [Leo].<div eID="gen38928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the veil--</hi>As the veil had to be passed through in order to enter the holiest place, so the weak, human suffering flesh (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>) of Christ's humanity (which veiled His God head) had to be passed through by Him in entering the heavenly holiest place for us; in putting off His rent flesh, the temple veil, its type, was simultaneously rent from top to bottom (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.51">Mt 27:51</reference>). Not His body, but His weak suffering flesh, was the veil; His body was the temple (<reference osisRef="John.2.19">Joh 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen38929" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7224fc85fd3be97f6468c21a588f8081a6b0a1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18507"/><div sID="gen38930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18507"/><hi type="bold">21. high priest--</hi>As a different Greek term (archiereus) is used always elsewhere in this Epistle for "high priest," translate as Greek here, "A Great Priest"; one who is at once King and "Priest on His throne" (<reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zec 6:13</reference>); a royal Priest, and a priestly King.<div eID="gen38930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of God--</hi>the spiritual house, the Church, made up of believers, whose home is heaven, where Jesus now is (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.23">23</reference>). Thus, by "the house of God," over which Jesus is, heaven is included in meaning, as well as the Church, whose home it is. <div eID="gen38931" type="x-p"/>
entries.e45c15ecfdaf827027fdb724920afd59cde88d3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18508"/><div sID="gen38932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18508"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">He 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.7.19">7:19</reference>.)<div eID="gen38932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a true heart--</hi>without hypocrisy; "in truth, and with a perfect heart"; a heart thoroughly imbued with "the truth" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">He 10:26</reference>).<div eID="gen38933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38934" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full assurance--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.6.11">He 6:11</reference>); with no doubt as to our acceptance when coming to God by the blood of Christ. As "faith" occurs here, so "hope," and "love," <reference osisRef="Heb.10.23">He 10:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.24">24</reference>.<div eID="gen38934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sprinkled from--</hi>that is, sprinkled so as to be cleansed from.<div eID="gen38935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38936" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil conscience--</hi>a consciousness of guilt unatoned for, and uncleansed away (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.2">He 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9">He 9:9</reference>). Both the hearts and the bodies are cleansed. The legal purifications were with blood of animal victims and with water, and could only cleanse the flesh (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.21">21</reference>). Christ's blood purifies the heart and conscience. The Aaronic priest, in entering the holy place, washed with water (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.19">He 9:19</reference>) in the brazen laver. Believers, as priests to God, are once for all washed in BODY (as distinguished from "hearts") at baptism. As we have an immaterial, and a material nature, the cleansing of both is expressed by "hearts" and "body," the inner and the outer man; so the whole man, material and immaterial. The baptism of the body, however, is not the mere putting away of material filth, nor an act operating by intrinsic efficacy, but the sacramental seal, applied to the outer man, of a spiritual washing (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.21">1Pe 3:21</reference>). "Body" (not merely "flesh," the carnal part, as <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.1">2Co 7:1</reference>) includes the whole material man, which needs cleansing, as being redeemed, as well as the soul. The body, once polluted with sin, is washed, so as to be fitted like Christ's holy body, and by His body, to be spiritually a pure and living offering. On the "pure water," the symbol of consecration and sanctification, compare <reference osisRef="John.19.34">Joh 19:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.6">1Jo 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">Eze 36:25</reference>. The perfects "having ... hearts sprinkled ... body (the Greek is singular) washed," imply a continuing state produced by a once-for-all accomplished act, namely, our justification by faith through Christ's blood, and consecration to God, sealed sacramentally by the baptism of our body. <div eID="gen38936" type="x-p"/>
entries.c22f72b162267a01bcccb2ba0a67b1b7914ab79c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18509"/><div sID="gen38937" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18509"/>23. (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">He 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.14">4:14</reference>.)<div eID="gen38937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38938" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profession--</hi>Greek, "confession."<div eID="gen38938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38939" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our faith--</hi>rather as Greek, "our hope"; which is indeed faith exercised as to the future inheritance. Hope rests on faith, and at the same time quickens faith, and is the ground of our bold confession (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1Pe 3:15</reference>). Hope is similarly (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">He 10:22</reference>) connected with purification (<reference osisRef="1John.3.3">1Jo 3:3</reference>).<div eID="gen38939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38940" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without wavering--</hi>without declension (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.14">He 3:14</reference>), "steadfast unto the end."<div eID="gen38940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God is faithful to His promises (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.17">He 6:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.11">11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">12:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.24">1Th 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.3">2Th 3:3</reference>; see also Christ's promise, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">Joh 12:26</reference>); but man is too often unfaithful to his duties. <div eID="gen38941" type="x-p"/>
entries.2678d26ad4eaaa8d0cada5abd6495f7f691510bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18510"/><div sID="gen38942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18510"/>24. Here, as elsewhere, hope and love follow faith; the Pauline triad of Christian graces.<div eID="gen38942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">consider--</hi>with the mind attentively fixed on "one another" (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.3.1">He 3:1</reference>), contemplating with continual consideration the characters and wants of our brethren, so as to render mutual help and counsel. Compare "consider," <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Psa 41:1</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>, "(All) looking diligently lest any fail of the grace of God."<div eID="gen38943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38944" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to provoke--</hi>Greek, "with a view to provoking unto love," instead of provoking to hatred, as is too often the case. <div eID="gen38944" type="x-p"/>
entries.0526976f9e764624e955856372fc240e09be0e2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18511"/><div sID="gen38945" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18511"/><hi type="bold">25. assembling of ourselves together--</hi>The Greek, "episunagoge," is only found here and <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1">2Th 2:1</reference> (the gathering together of the elect to Christ at His coming, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">Mt 24:31</reference>). The assembling or gathering of ourselves for Christian communion in private and public, is an earnest of our being gathered together to Him at His appearing. Union is strength; continual assemblings together beget and foster love, and give good opportunities for "provoking to good works," by "exhorting one another" (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.13">He 3:13</reference>). Ignatius says, "When ye frequently, and in numbers meet together, the powers of Satan are overthrown, and his mischief is neutralized by your likemindedness in the faith." To neglect such assemblings together might end in apostasy at last. He avoids the Greek term "sunagoge," as suggesting the Jewish synagogue meetings (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.2.9">Re 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen38945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the manner of some is--</hi>"manner," that is, habit, custom. This gentle expression proves he is not here as yet speaking of apostasy.<div eID="gen38946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day approaching--</hi>This, the shortest designation of the day of the Lord's coming, occurs elsewhere only in <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13">1Co 3:13</reference>; a confirmation of the Pauline authorship of this Epistle. The Church being in all ages kept uncertain how soon Christ is coming, the day is, and has been, in each age, practically always near; whence, believers have been called on always to be watching for it as nigh at hand. The Hebrews were now living close upon One of those great types and foretastes of it, the destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.1">Mt 24:1</reference>, 2), "the bloody and fiery dawn of the great day; that day is the day of days, the ending day of all days, the settling day of all days, the day of the promotion of time into eternity, the day which, for the Church, breaks through and breaks off the night of the present world" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <div eID="gen38947" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0dfdd1b48516b2e58e752fe04c216409ef073c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18512"/><div sID="gen38948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18512"/>26. Compare on this and following verses, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>, &c. There the warning was that if there be not diligence in progressing, a falling off will take place, and apostasy may ensue: here it is, that if there be lukewarmness in Christian communion, apostasy may ensue.<div eID="gen38948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if we sin--</hi>Greek present participle: if we be found sinning, that is, not isolated acts, but a state of sin [Alford]. A violation not only of the law, but of the whole economy of the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.28">He 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">29</reference>).<div eID="gen38949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilfully--</hi>presumptuously, Greek "willingly." After receiving "full knowledge (so the Greek, compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>) of the truth," by having been "enlightened," and by having "tasted" a certain measure even of grace of "the Holy Ghost" (the Spirit of truth, <reference osisRef="John.14.17">Joh 14:17</reference>; and "the Spirit of grace," <reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">He 10:29</reference>): to fall away (as "sin" here means, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.12">He 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.17">17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.6.6">He 6:6</reference>) and apostatize (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.12">He 3:12</reference>) to Judaism or infidelity, is not a sin of ignorance, or error ("out of the way," the result) of infirmity, but a deliberate sinning against the Spirit (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.29">He 10:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.2">He 5:2</reference>): such sinning, where a consciousness of Gospel obligations not only was, but is present: a sinning presumptuously and preseveringly against Christ's redemption for us, and the Spirit of grace in us. "He only who stands high can fall low. A lively reference in the soul to what is good is necessary in order to be thoroughly wicked; hence, man can be more reprobate than the beasts, and the apostate angels than apostate man" [Tholuck].<div eID="gen38950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remaineth no more sacrifice--</hi>For there is but ONE Sacrifice that can atone for sin; they, after having fully known that sacrifice, deliberately reject it. <div eID="gen38951" type="x-p"/>
entries.7374dee242acdb64a6ee2c25245de89fdc7d94ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18513"/><div sID="gen38952" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18513"/><hi type="bold">27. a certain--</hi>an extraordinary and indescribable. The indefiniteness, as of something peculiar of its kind, makes the description the more terrible (compare Greek, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">Jas 1:18</reference>).<div eID="gen38952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38953" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">looking for--</hi>"expectation": a later sense of the Greek. Alford strangely translates, as the Greek usually means elsewhere, "reception." The transition is easy from "giving a reception to" something or someone, to "looking for." Contrast the "expecting" (the very same Greek as here), <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13">He 10:13</reference>, which refutes Alford.<div eID="gen38953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fiery indignation--</hi>literally, "zeal of fire." Fire is personified: glow or ardor of fire, that is, of Him who is "a consuming fire."<div eID="gen38954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour--</hi>continually. <div eID="gen38955" type="x-p"/>
entries.38ba6d28952a5277af7102c11e4398f272311ff8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18514"/><div sID="gen38956" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18514"/>28. Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>; 12:25.<div eID="gen38956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despised--</hi>"set at naught" [Alford]: utterly and heinously violated, not merely some minor detail, but the whole law and covenant; for example, by idolatry (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7">De 17:2-7</reference>). So here apostasy answers to such an utter violation of the old covenant.<div eID="gen38957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">died--</hi>Greek, "dies": the normal punishment of such transgression, then still in force.<div eID="gen38958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without mercy--</hi>literally, "mercies": removal out of the pale of mitigation, or a respite of his doom.<div eID="gen38959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under--</hi>on the evidence of. <div eID="gen38960" type="x-p"/>
entries.22ed2ccd77b98b3e9a612cf205af6021b2d78c77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18515"/><div sID="gen38961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18515"/><hi type="bold">29. sorer--</hi>Greek, "worse," namely, "punishment" (literally, "vengeance") than any mere temporal punishment of the body.<div eID="gen38961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suppose ye--</hi>an appeal to the Hebrews' reason and conscience.<div eID="gen38962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thought worthy--</hi>by God at the judgment.<div eID="gen38963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trodden under foot the Son of God--</hi>by "wilful" apostasy. So he treads under foot God Himself who "glorified His Son as an high priest" (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.5">He 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.6">6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen38964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an unholy thing--</hi>literally, "common," as opposed to "sanctified." No better than the blood of a common man, thus involving the consequence that Christ, in claiming to be God, was guilty of blasphemy, and so deserved to die!<div eID="gen38965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wherewith he was sanctified--</hi>for Christ died even for him. "Sanctified," in the fullest sense, belongs only to the saved elect. But in some sense it belongs also to those who have gone a far way in Christian experience, and yet fall away at last. The higher such a one's past Christian experiences, the deeper his fall.<div eID="gen38966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">done despite unto--</hi>by repelling in fact: as "blasphemy" is despite in words (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.29">Mr 3:29</reference>). "Of the Jews who became Christians and relapsed to Judaism, we find from the history of Uriel Acosta, that they required a blasphemy against Christ. 'They applied to Him epithets used against Molech the adulterous branch,' &c." [Tholuck].<div eID="gen38967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Spirit of grace--</hi>the Spirit that confers grace. "He who does not accept the benefit, insults Him who confers it. He hath made thee a son: wilt thou become a slave? He has come to take up His abode with thee; but thou art introducing evil into thyself" [Chrysostom]. "It is the curse of evil eternally to propagate evil: so, for him who profanes the Christ without him, and blasphemes the Christ within him, there is subjectively no renewal of a change of mind (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.6">He 6:6</reference>), and objectively no new sacrifice for sins" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">He 10:26</reference>) [Tholuck]. <div eID="gen38968" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8fc39f5590e8f3cc0e292fb510289ea28aa8712: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18516"/><div sID="gen38969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18516"/><hi type="bold">30. him--</hi>God, who enters no empty threats.<div eID="gen38969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Vengeance belongeth unto me--</hi>Greek, "To Me belongeth vengeance": exactly according with Paul's quotation, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">Ro 12:19</reference>, of the same text.<div eID="gen38970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord shall judge his people--</hi>in grace, or else anger, according as each deserves: here, "judge," so as to punish the reprobate apostate; there, "judge," so as to interpose in behalf of, and save His people (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">De 32:36</reference>). <div eID="gen38971" type="x-p"/>
entries.e894c51b67a71a97e1bdd88fbac8713c297ae9fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18517"/><div sID="gen38972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18517"/><hi type="bold">31. fearful ... to fall into the hands--</hi>It is good like David to fall into the hands of God, rather than man, when one does so with filial faith in his father's love, though God chastises him. "It is fearful" to fall into His hands as a reprobate and presumptuous sinner doomed to His just vengeance as Judge (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.27">He 10:27</reference>).<div eID="gen38972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living God--</hi>therefore able to punish for ever (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.28">Mt 10:28</reference>). <div eID="gen38973" type="x-p"/>
entries.1651530b7a4a1c82fbb96f4dd4514875e2666a1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18518"/><div sID="gen38974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18518"/>32. As previously he has warned them by the awful end of apostates, so here he stirs them up by the remembrance of their own former faith, patience, and self-sacrificing love. So <reference osisRef="Rev.2.3">Re 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>.<div eID="gen38974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call to remembrance--</hi>habitually: so the present tense means.<div eID="gen38975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">illuminated--</hi>"enlightened": come to "the knowledge of the truth" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26">He 10:26</reference>) in connection with baptism (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4">He 6:4</reference>). In spiritual baptism, Christ, who is "the Light," is put on. "On the one hand, we are not to sever the sign and the grace signified where the sacrifice truly answers its designs; on the other, the glass is not to be mistaken for the liquor, nor the sheath for the sword" [Bengel].<div eID="gen38976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fight of--</hi>that is, consisting of afflictions. <div eID="gen38977" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e8a541f00060fbc8fbef5c746289e834b246eb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18519"/><div sID="gen38978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18519"/>33. The persecutions here referred to seem to have been endured by the Hebrew Christians at their first conversion, not only in Palestine, but also in Rome and elsewhere, the Jews in every city inciting the populace and the Roman authorities against Christians.<div eID="gen38978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gazing-stock--</hi>as in a theater (so the Greek): often used as the place of punishment in the presence of the assembled multitudes. <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">Ac 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Co 4:9</reference>, "Made a theatrical spectacle to the world."<div eID="gen38979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye became--</hi>of your own accord: attesting your Christian sympathy with your suffering brethren.<div eID="gen38980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">companions of--</hi>sharers in affliction with. <div eID="gen38981" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5a921c90b5983642e69385f7e023c0096020028: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18520"/><div sID="gen38982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18520"/><hi type="bold">34. ye had compassion on me in my bonds--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and versions omit "me," and read, "Ye both sympathized with those in bonds (answering to the last clause of <reference osisRef="Heb.10.33">He 10:33</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.3">He 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">6:10</reference>), and accepted (so the Greek is translated in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">He 11:35</reference>) with joy (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.2">Jas 1:2</reference>; joy in tribulations, as exercising faith and other graces, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>; and the pledge of the coming glory, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">Mt 5:12</reference>) the plundering of your (own) goods (answering to the first clause of <reference osisRef="Heb.10.33">He 10:33</reference>)."<div eID="gen38982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in yourselves--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "in": translate, "knowing that ye have for (or 'to') yourselves."<div eID="gen38983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">better--</hi>a heavenly (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">He 11:16</reference>).<div eID="gen38984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enduring--</hi>not liable to spoiling.<div eID="gen38985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">substance--</hi>possession: peculiarly our own, if we will not cast away our birthright. <div eID="gen38986" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0a0c910de68ca9414ed5ec0664dfe5504a322e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18521"/><div sID="gen38987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18521"/>35-37. Consequent exhortation to confidence and endurance, as Christ is soon coming.<div eID="gen38987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Cast not away--</hi>implying that they now have "confidence," and that it will not withdraw of itself, unless they "cast it away" wilfully (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.3.14">He 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen38988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which--</hi>Greek, "the which": inasmuch as being such as.<div eID="gen38989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath--</hi>present tense: it is as certain as if you had it in your hand (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.37">He 10:37</reference>). It hath in reversion.<div eID="gen38990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen38991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">recompense of reward--</hi>of grace not of debt: a reward of a kind which no mercenary self-seeker would seek: holiness will be its own reward; self-devoting unselfishness for Christ's sake will be its own rich recompense (see on <reference osisRef="Heb.2.2">He 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.26">He 11:26</reference>). <div eID="gen38991" type="x-p"/>
entries.10e81ec29b5967d6f6ecbbc59d6189a5d9a6b97e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18525"/><div sID="gen39000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18525"/>39. A Pauline elegant turning-off from denunciatory warnings to charitable hopes of his readers (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.12">Ro 8:12</reference>).<div eID="gen39000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saving of the soul--</hi>literally, "acquisition (or obtaining) of the soul." The kindred Greek verb is applied to Christ's acquiring the Church as the purchase of His blood (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>). If we acquire or obtain our soul's salvation, it is through Him who has obtained it for us by His bloodshedding. "The unbelieving man loses his soul: for not being God's, neither is he his own [compare <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>, with Lu 9:25]: faith saves the soul by linking it to God" [Delitzsch in Alford]. <chapter eID="Heb.10"/>

entries.ec0fbb385612122d305746d281e9dbd056fb4ffa: <div eID="gen53506" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen53507" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53508" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53508" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53507" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53509" type="x-p"/> The insufficiency of the legal sacrifices to take away sin, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.1-Heb.10.4">Heb 10:1-4</reference>. The purpose and will of God, as declared by the Psalmist, relative to the salvation of the world by the incarnation of Christ; and our sanctification through that will, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.5-Heb.10.10">Heb 10:5-10</reference>. Comparison between the priesthood of Christ and that of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.11-Heb.10.14">Heb 10:11-14</reference>. The new covenant which God promised to make, and the blessings of it, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.15-Heb.10.17">Heb 10:15-17</reference>. The access which genuine believers have to the holiest by the blood of Jesus, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.18-Heb.10.20">Heb 10:18-20</reference>. Having a High Priest over the Church of God, we should have faith, walk uprightly, hold fast our profession, exhort and help each other, and maintain Christian communion, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.21-Heb.10.25">Heb 10:21-25</reference>. The danger and awful consequences of final apostasy, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.31">Heb 10:26-31</reference>. In order to our perseverance, we should often reflect on past mercies, and the support afforded us in temptations and afflictions; and not cast away our confidence, for we shall receive the promise if we patiently fulfill the will of God, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.32-Heb.10.37">Heb 10:32-37</reference>. The just by faith shall live; but the soul that draws back shall die, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb 10:38</reference>. The apostle's confidence in the believing Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">Heb 10:39</reference>. <div eID="gen53509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen53510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53511" type="x-p"/> The law, having a shadow of good things to come - A shadow, σκια, signifies, <div eID="gen53511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53512" type="x-p"/> 1. Literally, the shade cast from a body of any kind, interposed between the place on which the shadow is projected, and the sun or light; the rays of the light not shining on that place, because intercepted by the opacity of the body, through which they cannot pass. <div eID="gen53512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53513" type="x-p"/> 2. It signifies, technically, a sketch, rude plan, or imperfect draught of a building, landscape, man, beast, etc. <div eID="gen53513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53514" type="x-p"/> 3. It signifies, metaphorically, any faint adumbration, symbolical expression, imperfect or obscure image of a thing; and is opposed to σωμα, body, or the thing intended to be thereby defined. <div eID="gen53514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53515" type="x-p"/> 4. It is used catachrestically among the Greek writers, as umbra is among the Latins, to signify any thing vain, empty, light, not solid; thus Philostratus, Vit. Soph., lib. i. cap. 20: Ὁτι σκια και ονειρατα αἱ ἡδοναι πασαι· All pleasures are but Shadows and dreams. And Cicero, in Pison., cap. 24: Omnes umbras falsae gloriae consectari. "All pursue the Shadows of False Glory." And again, De Offic., lib. iii. cap. 17: Nos veri juris germanaeque justitiae solidam et expressam effigiem nullam tenemus; umbra et itnaginibus utimur. "We have no solid and express effigy of true law and genuine justice, but we employ shadows and images to represent them." <div eID="gen53515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53516" type="x-p"/> And not the very image - Εικων, image, signifies, <div eID="gen53516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53517" type="x-p"/> 1. A simple representation, from εικω, I am like. <div eID="gen53517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53518" type="x-p"/> 2. The form or particular fashion of a thing. <div eID="gen53518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53519" type="x-p"/> 3. The model according to which any thing is formed. <div eID="gen53519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53520" type="x-p"/> 4. The perfect image of a thing as opposed to a faint representation. <div eID="gen53520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53521" type="x-p"/> 5. Metaphorically, a similitude, agreement, or conformity. <div eID="gen53521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53522" type="x-p"/> The law, with all its ceremonies and sacrifices, was only a shadow of spiritual and eternal good. The Gospel is the image or thing itself, as including every spiritual and eternal good. <div eID="gen53522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53523" type="x-p"/> We may note three things here: <div eID="gen53523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53524" type="x-p"/> 1. The shadow or general outline, limiting the size and proportions of the thing to be represented. <div eID="gen53524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53525" type="x-p"/> 2. The image or likeness completed from this shadow or general outline, whether represented on paper, canvass, or in statuary, <div eID="gen53525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53526" type="x-p"/> 3. The person or thing thus represented in its actual, natural state of existence; or what is called here the very image of the things, αυτην την εικονα των πραγματων. <div eID="gen53526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53527" type="x-p"/> Such is the Gospel, when compared with the law; such is Christ, when compared with Aaron; such is his sacrifice, when compared with the Levitical offerings; such is the Gospel remission of sins and purification, when compared with those afforded by the law; such is the Holy Ghost, ministered by the Gospel, when compared with its types and shadows in the Levitical service; such the heavenly rest, when compared with the earthly Canaan. Well, therefore, might the apostle say, The law was only the shadow of good things to come. <div eID="gen53527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53528" type="x-p"/> Can never - make the comers thereunto perfect - Cannot remove guilt from the conscience, or impurity from the heart. I leave preachers to improve these points.
entries.7a0312500c84e54e60a168f1afbbe959d60ddd7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen53528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53529" type="x-p"/> Would they not have ceased to be offered? - Had they made an effectual reconciliation for the sins of the world, and contained in their once offering a plenitude of permanent merit, they would have ceased to be offered, at least in reference to any individual who had once offered them; because, in such a case, his conscience would be satisfied that its guilt had been taken away. But no Jew pretended to believe that even the annual atonement cancelled his sin before God; yet he continued to make his offerings, the law of God having so enjoined, because these sacrifices pointed out that which was to come. They were offered, therefore, not in consideration of their own efficacy, but as referring to Christ; See on <reference osisRef="Heb.9.9">Heb 9:9</reference> (note).
entries.e58603c703594075a16b559e39c55b0b3e6ec4c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen53529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53530" type="x-p"/> For it is not possible - Common sense must have taught them that shedding the blood of bulls and goats could never satisfy Divine justice, nor take away guilt from the conscience; and God intended that they should understand the matter so: and this the following quotation from the Psalmist sufficiently proves.
entries.cd636dd24a5ec06a974929e1444d203527a02dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen53530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53531" type="x-p"/> When he (the Messiah) cometh into the world - Was about to be incarnated, He saith to God the Father, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not - it was never thy will and design that the sacrifices under thy own law should be considered as making atonement for sin, they were only designed to point out my incarnation and consequent sacrificial death, and therefore a body hast thou prepared me, by a miraculous conception in the womb of a virgin, according to thy word, The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent. <div eID="gen53531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53532" type="x-p"/> A body hast thou prepared me - The quotation in this and the two following verses is taken from Psalm 40, 6th, 7th, and 8th verses, as they stand now in the Septuagint, with scarcely any variety of reading; but, although the general meaning is the same, they are widely different in verbal expression in the Hebrew. David's words are, אזנים כרית לי oznayim caritha li, which we translate, My ears hast thou opened; but they might be more properly rendered, My ears hast thou bored, that is, thou hast made me thy servant for ever, to dwell in thine own house; for the allusion is evidently to the custom mentioned, <reference osisRef="Exo.21.2">Exo 21:2</reference>, etc.: "If thou buy a Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free; but if the servant shall positively say, I love my master, etc., I will not go out free, then his master shall bring him to the door post, and shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall serve him for ever." But how is it possible that the Septuagint and the apostle should take a meaning so totally different from the sense of the Hebrew? Dr. Kennicott has a very ingenious conjecture here: he supposes that the Septuagint and apostle express the meaning of the words as they stood in the copy from which the Greek translation was made; and that the present Hebrew text is corrupted in the word אזנים oznayim, ears, which has been written through carelessness for אז גוה az gevah, Then a Body. The first syllable אז, Then, is the same in both; and the latter נים, which joined to אז, makes אזנים oznayim, might have been easily mistaken for גוה gevah, Body; נ nun, being very like ג gimel; י yod, like ו vau; and ה he, like final ם mem; especially if the line on which the letters were written in the MS. happened to be blacker than ordinary, which has often been a cause of mistake, it might have been easily taken for the under stroke of the mem, and thus give rise to a corrupt reading: add to this the root כרה carah, signifies as well to prepare as to open, bore, etc. On this supposition the ancient copy, translated by the Septuagint, and followed by the apostle, must have read the text thus: אז גוה כרית לי az gevah caritha li, σωμα δε κατηρτισω μοι, then a body thou hast prepared me: thus the Hebrew text, the version of the Septuagint, and the apostle, will agree in what is known to be an indisputable fact in Christianity, namely, that Christ was incarnated for the sin of the world. <div eID="gen53532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53533" type="x-p"/> The Ethiopic has nearly the same reading; the Arabic has both, A body hast thou prepared me, and mine ears thou hast opened. But the Syriac, the Chaldee, and the Vulgate, agree with the present Hebrew text; and none of the MSS. collated by Kennicott and De Rossi have any various reading on the disputed words. <div eID="gen53533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53534" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable that all the offerings and sacrifices which were considered to be of an atoning or cleansing nature, offered under the law, are here enumerated by the psalmist and the apostle, to show that none of them nor all of them could take away sin, and that the grand sacrifice of Christ was that alone which could do it. <div eID="gen53534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53535" type="x-p"/> Four kinds are here specified, both by the psalmist and the apostle, viz.: <div eID="gen53535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53536" type="x-p"/> Sacrifice, זבח zebach, θυσια· <div eID="gen53536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53537" type="x-p"/> Offering, מנחה minchah, προσφορα· <div eID="gen53537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53538" type="x-p"/> Burnt-Offering, עולה olah, ὁλοκαυτωμα· <div eID="gen53538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53539" type="x-p"/> Sin-Offering, חטאה chataah, περι ἁμαρτιας. <div eID="gen53539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53540" type="x-p"/> Of all these we may say, with the apostle, it was impossible that the blood of bulls and goats, etc., should take away sin.
entries.6d2cb7857587150628fa5aed40fd9e0f0c7ba8f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen53540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53541" type="x-p"/> Thou hast had no pleasure - Thou couldst never be pleased with the victims under the law; thou couldst never consider them as atonements for sin; as they could never satisfy thy justice, nor make thy law honorable.
entries.b3afe0c6ae082ac587e329a0b19247966f3ffcb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen53541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53542" type="x-p"/> In the volume of the book - במגלת ספר bimgillath sepher, "in the roll of the book." Anciently, books were written on skins and rolled up. Among the Romans these were called volumina, from volvo, I roll; and the Pentateuch, in the Jewish synagogues, is still written in this way. There are two wooden rollers; on one they roll on, on the other they roll off, as they proceed in reading. The book mentioned here must be the Pentateuch, or five books of Moses; for in David's time no other part of Divine revelation had been committed to writing. This whole book speaks about Christ, and his accomplishing the will of God; not only in, The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent, and, In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, but in all the sacrifices and sacrificial rites mentioned in the law. <div eID="gen53542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53543" type="x-p"/> To do thy will - God willed not the sacrifices under the law, but he willed that a human victim of infinite merit should be offered for the redemption of mankind. That there might be such a victim, a body was prepared for the eternal Logos; and in that body he came to do the will of God, that is, to suffer and die for the sins of the world.
entries.4794b83691601933d8f91b30ec015efe02330b0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen53543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53544" type="x-p"/> He taketh away the first - The offerings, sacrifices, burnt-offerings, and sacrifices for sin, which were prescribed by the law. <div eID="gen53544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53545" type="x-p"/> That he may establish the second - The offering of the body of Jesus once for all. It will make little odds in the meaning if we say, he taketh away the first covenant, that he may establish the second covenant; he takes away the first dispensation, that he may establish the second; he takes away the law, that he may establish the Gospel. In all these cases the sense is nearly the same: I prefer the first.
entries.a63ad1dde87303748423d4af29d25e9cefe7d1f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen53545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53546" type="x-p"/> By the which will we are sanctified - Closing in with this so solemnly declared Will of God, that there is no name given under heaven among men, by which we can be saved, but Jesus the Christ, we believe in him, find redemption in his blood, and are sanctified unto God through the sacrificial offering of his body. <div eID="gen53546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53547" type="x-p"/> 1. Hence we see that the sovereign Will of God is, that Jesus should be incarnated; that he should suffer and die, or, in the apostle's words, taste death for every man; that all should believe on him, and be saved from their sins: for this is the Will of God, our sanctification. <div eID="gen53547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53548" type="x-p"/> 2. And as the apostle grounds this on the words of the psalm, we see that it is the Will of God that that system shall end; for as the essence of it is contained in its sacrifices, and God says he will not have these, and has prepared the Messiah to do his will, i.e. to die for men, hence it necessarily follows, from the psalmist himself, that the introduction of the Messiah into the world is the abolition of the law, and that his sacrifice is that which shall last for ever.
entries.7402ed8d7e7d19e52a4d292fa85c9c881a1c024a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen53548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53549" type="x-p"/> Every priest standeth - The office of the Jewish priest is here compared with the office of our High Priest. The Jewish priest stands daily at the altar, like a servant ministering, repeating the same sacrifices; our High Priest offered himself once for all, and sat down at the right hand of God, as the only-begotten Son and Heir of all things, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.12">Heb 10:12</reference>. This continual offering argued the imperfection of the sacrifices. Our Lord's once offering, proves his was complete.
entries.d25d800a08d948ee32a0499ddb645fafec720123: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen53549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53550" type="x-p"/> Till his enemies be made his footstool - Till all that oppose his high priesthood and sacrificial offering shall be defeated, routed, and confounded; and acknowledge, in their punishment, the supremacy of his power as universal and eternal King, who refused to receive him as their atoning and sanctifying Priest. There is also an oblique reference here to the destruction of the Jews, which was then at hand; for Christ was about to take away the second with an overwhelming flood of desolations.
entries.d12c7c1c54dabd83ae28401c82da4cbbbb8aaf5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen53550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53551" type="x-p"/> For by one offering - His death upon the cross. <div eID="gen53551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53552" type="x-p"/> He hath perfected for ever - He has procured remission of sins and holiness; fur it is well observed here, and in several parts of this epistle, that τελειοω, to make perfect, is the same as αφεσιν ἁμαρτιων ποιεω, to procure remission of sins. <div eID="gen53552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53553" type="x-p"/> Them that are sanctified - Τους ἁγιαζομενους· Them that have received the sprinkling of the blood of this offering. These, therefore, receiving redemption through that blood, have no need of any other offering; as this was a complete atonement, purification, and title to eternal glory.
entries.01f6dc5595218dcd5a57c3a3a3146214c0939c5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen53553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53554" type="x-p"/> The Holy Ghost - is a witness to us - The words are quoted from <reference osisRef="Jer.31.33">Jer 31:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jer 31:34</reference>, and here we are assured that Jeremiah spoke by the inspiration of the Spirit of God. Had said before - See <reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.12">Heb 8:12</reference>, and the notes there.
entries.484c30df59be6767d260c7140f4128c85bb6da5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen53554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53555" type="x-p"/> Now where remission of these is - In any case, where sin is once pardoned, there is no farther need of a sin-offering; but every believer on Christ has his sin blotted out, and therefore needs no other offering for that sin. "If," says Dr. Macknight, "after remission is granted to the sinner, there is no need of any more sacrifice for sin; and if Christ, by offering himself once, has perfected for ever the sanctified, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.14">Heb 10:14</reference>, the sacrifice of the mass, as it is called, about which the Romish clergy employ themselves so incessantly, and to which the papists trust for the pardon of their sins, has no foundation in Scripture. Nay, it is an evident impiety, as it proceeds upon the supposition that the offering of the body of Christ once is not sufficient to procure the pardon of sin, but must be frequently repeated. If they reply that their mass is only the representation and commemoration of the sacrifice of Christ, they give up the cause, and renounce an article of their faith, established by the council of Trent, which, in session xxii. can. 1, 3, declared the sacrifice of the mass to be a true and propitiatory sacrifice for sin. I say, give up the cause; for the representation and commemoration of a sacrifice is not a sacrifice. Farther, it cannot be affirmed that the body of Christ is offered in the mass, unless it can be said that, as often as it is offered, Christ has suffered death; for the apostle says expressly, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.25">Heb 9:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb 9:26</reference>, that if Christ offered himself often, he must often have suffered since the foundation of the world." Let him disprove this who can.
entries.e3cb23b8ce9cfe52be4b995c83f6b16c9559445a: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen53555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53556" type="x-p"/> Having therefore, brethren, boldness - The apostle, having now finished the doctrinal part of his epistle, and fully shown the superiority of Christ to all men and angels, and the superiority of his priesthood to that of Aaron and his successors, the absolute inefficacy of the Jewish sacrifices to make atonement for sin, and the absolute efficacy of that of Christ to make reconciliation of man to God, proceeds now to show what influence these doctrines should have on the hearts and lives of those who believe in his merits and death. <div eID="gen53556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53557" type="x-p"/> Boldness to enter - Παρῥησιαν εις την εισοδον· Liberty, full access to the entrance of the holy place, των ἁγιων· This is an allusion to the case of the high priest going into the holy of holies. He went with fear and trembling, because, if he had neglected the smallest item prescribed by the law, he could expect nothing but death. Genuine believers can come even to the throne of God with confidence, as they carry into the Divine presence the infinitely meritorious blood of the great atonement; and, being justified through that blood, they have a right to all the blessings of the eternal kingdom.
entries.cc4952d6ab3a90287846cf58e96fc0e2c708be67: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen53557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53558" type="x-p"/> By a new and living way - It is a new way; no human being had ever before entered into the heaven of heavens; Jesus in human nature was the first, and thus he has opened the way to heaven to mankind, his own resurrection and ascension to glory being the proof and pledge of ours. <div eID="gen53558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53559" type="x-p"/> The way is called ὁδον προσφατον και ζωσαν, new or fresh, and living. This is evidently an allusion to the blood of the victim newly shed, uncoagulated, and consequently proper to be used for sprinkling. The blood of the Jewish victims was fit for sacrificial purposes only so long as it was warm and fluid, and might be considered as yet possessing its vitality; but when it grew cold, it coagulated, lost its vitality, and was no longer proper to be used sacrificially. Christ is here, in the allusion, represented as newly slain, and yet living; the blood ever considered as flowing and giving life to the world. The way by the old covenant neither gave life, nor removed the liability to death. The way to peace and reconciliation, under the old covenant, was through the dead bodies of the animals slain; but Christ is living, and ever liveth, to make intercession for us; therefore he is a new and living way. <div eID="gen53559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53560" type="x-p"/> In the Choephorae of Aeschylus, ver. 801, there is an expression like this of the apostle: - Αγετε, των παλαι πεπραγμενων Αυσασθ' ἁιμα προσφατοις δικαις. <div eID="gen53560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53561" type="x-p"/> Agite, olim venditorum <div eID="gen53561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53562" type="x-p"/> Solvite sanguinem recenti vindicta. <div eID="gen53562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53563" type="x-p"/> This way, says Dr. Owen, is new, <div eID="gen53563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53564" type="x-p"/> 1. Because it was but newly made and prepared. <div eID="gen53564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53565" type="x-p"/> 2. Because it belongs unto the new covenant. <div eID="gen53565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53566" type="x-p"/> 3. Because it admits of no decays, but is always new, as to its efficacy and use, as in the day of its first preparation. <div eID="gen53566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53567" type="x-p"/> 4. The way of the tabernacle waxed old, and so was prepared for a removal; but the Gospel way of salvation shall never be altered, nor changed, nor decay; it is always new, and remains for ever. <div eID="gen53567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53568" type="x-p"/> It is also called ζωσαν, living, <div eID="gen53568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53569" type="x-p"/> 1. In opposition to the way into the holiest under the tabernacle, which was by death; nothing could be done in it without the blood of a victim. <div eID="gen53569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53570" type="x-p"/> 2. It was the cause of death to any who might use it, except the high priest himself; and he could have access to it only one day in the year. <div eID="gen53570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53571" type="x-p"/> 3. It is called living, because it has a spiritual vital efficacy in our access to God. <div eID="gen53571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53572" type="x-p"/> 4. It is living as to its effects; it leads to life, and infallibly brings those who walk in it unto life eternal. <div eID="gen53572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53573" type="x-p"/> Through the veil - As the high priest lifted up or drew aside the veil that separated the holy from the most holy place, in order that he might have access to the Divine Majesty; and as the veil of the temple was rent from the top to the bottom at the crucifixion of Christ, to show that the way to the holiest was then laid open; so we must approach the throne through the mediation of Christ, and through his sacrificial death. His pierced side is the way to the holiest. Here the veil - his humanity, is rent, and the kingdom of heaven opened to all believers.
entries.b2272e40f6c78fca552c647f63b43698401f4d79: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen53573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53574" type="x-p"/> A high priest over the house of God - The house or family of God is the Christian Church, or all true believers in the Lord Jesus. Over this Church, house, or family, Christ is the High Priest - in their behalf he offers his own blood, and their prayers and praises; and as the high priest had the ordering of all things that appertained to the house and worship of God, so has Christ in the government of his Church. This government he never gave into other hands. As none can govern and preserve the world but God, so none can govern and save the Church but the Lord Jesus: He is over the house; He is its President; he instructs, protects, guides, feeds, defends, and saves the flock. Those who have such a President may well have confidence; for with him is the fountain of life, and he has all power in the heavens and in the earth.
entries.5014e64c6d571e5d167f688e786de35d75000061: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen53574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53575" type="x-p"/> Let us draw near - Let us come with the blood of our sacrifice to the throne of God: the expression is sacrificial. <div eID="gen53575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53576" type="x-p"/> With a true heart - Deeply convinced of our need of help, and truly in earnest to obtain it. <div eID="gen53576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53577" type="x-p"/> In full assurance of faith - Being fully persuaded that God will accept us for the sake of his Son, and that the sacrificial death of Christ gives us full authority to expect every blessing we need. <div eID="gen53577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53578" type="x-p"/> Having our hearts sprinkled - Not our bodies, as was the case among the Hebrews, when they had contracted any pollution, for they were to be sprinkled with the water of separation, see <reference osisRef="Num.19.2-Num.19.10">Num 19:2-10</reference>; but our hearts, sprinkled by the cleansing efficacy of the blood of Christ, without which we cannot draw nigh to God. <div eID="gen53578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53579" type="x-p"/> From an evil conscience - Having that deep sense of guilt which our conscience felt taken all away, and the peace and love of God shed abroad ill our hearts by the Holy Ghost given unto us. <div eID="gen53579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53580" type="x-p"/> Our bodies washed with pure water - The high priest, before he entered into the inner tabernacle, or put on his holy garments, was to wash his flesh in water, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Lev 16:4</reference>, and the Levites were to be cleansed the same way, <reference osisRef="Num.8.7">Num 8:7</reference>. The apostle probably alludes to this in what he says here, though it appears that he refers principally to baptisms, the washing by which was an emblem of the purification of the soul by the grace and Spirit of Christ; but it is most likely that it is to the Jewish baptisms, and not the Christian, that the apostle alludes.
entries.364d3911dfa01ab34585ea4a3525ea156281b33a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen53580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53581" type="x-p"/> Let us hold fast the profession of our faith - The word ὁμολογια, from ὁμου, together, and λογος, a word, implies that general consent that was among Christians on all the important articles of their faith and practice; particularly their acknowledgment of the truth of the Gospel, and of Jesus Christ, as the only victim for sin, and the only Savior from it. If the word washed above refer to Christian baptism in the ease of adults, then the profession is that which the baptized then made of their faith in the Gospel; and of their determination to live and die in that faith. <div eID="gen53581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53582" type="x-p"/> The various readings on this clause are many in the MSS., etc. Της ελπιδος την ὁμολογιαν, the confession of our Hope; D*, two of the Itala, Vulgate, Erpen's Arabic, and the Ethiopic. Ὁμολογιαν της πιστεως, the confession of Faith; one of the Barberini MSS. and two others. This is the reading which our translators have followed; but it is of very little authority. Την επαγγελιαν της ελπιδος, the promise of Hope; St. Chrysostom. Την ελπιδα της ὁμολογιας, the Hope of our Profession; one of Petavius's MSS. But among all these, the confession or profession of Hope is undoubtedly the genuine reading. Now, among the primitive Christians, the hope which they professed was the resurrection of the body, and everlasting life; every thing among these Christians was done and believed in reference to a future state; and for the joy that this set before them, they, like their Master, endured every cross, and despised all shame: they expected to be with God, through Christ; this hope they professed to have; and they confessed boldly and publicly the faith on which this hope was built. The apostle exhorts them to hold fast this confession without wavering - never to doubt the declarations made to them by their Redeemer, but having the full assurance of faith that their hearts were sprinkled from an evil conscience, that they had found redemption in the blood of the lamb, they might expect to be glorified with their living Head in the kingdom of their Father. <div eID="gen53582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53583" type="x-p"/> He is faithful that promised - The eternal life, which is the object of your hope, is promised to you by him who cannot lie; as he then is faithful who has given you this promise, hold fast the profession of your hope.
entries.bbad4d40d89ac772bcdb7f5323ee23cf8a9fe690: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen53583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53584" type="x-p"/> And let us consider one another - Κατανοωμεν· Let us diligently and attentively consider each other's trials, difficulties, and weaknesses; feel for each other, and excite each other to an increase of love to God and man; and, as the proof of it, to be fruitful in good works. The words εις παροξυσμον, to the provocation, are often taken in a good sense, and signify excitement, stirring up, to do any thing laudable, useful, honorable, or necessary. Xenophon, Cyrop., lib. vi., page 108, speaking of the conduct of Cyrus towards his officers, says: Και τουτους επαινων τε, παρωξυνε, και χαριζομενος αυτοις ὁ τι δυναιτο. "He by praises and gifts excited them as much as possible." See the note on <reference osisRef="Act.15.39">Act 15:39</reference>, where the subject is farther considered.
entries.5fe0867a00be7d421651fb4f7559f2ace62aa7f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen53584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53585" type="x-p"/> Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves - Επισυναγωγην ἑαυτων. Whether this means public or private worship is hard to say; but as the word is but once more used in the New Testament, (<reference osisRef="2Thes.2.1">2Thes 2:1</reference>), and there means the gathering together of the redeemed of the Lord at the day of judgment, it is as likely that it means here private religious meetings, for the purpose of mutual exhortation: and this sense appears the more natural here, because it is evident that the Church was now in a state of persecution, and therefore their meetings were most probably held in private. For fear of persecution, it seems as if some had deserted these meetings, καθως εθος τισιν, as the custom of certain persons is. They had given up these strengthening and instructive means, and the others were in danger of following their example. <div eID="gen53585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53586" type="x-p"/> The day approaching - Την ἡμεραν· That day - the time in which God would come and pour out his judgments on the Jewish nation. We may also apply it to the day of death and the day of judgment. Both of these are approaching to every human being. He who wishes to be found ready will carefully use every means of grace, and particularly the communion of saints, if there be even but two or three in the place where he lives, who statedly meet together in the name of Christ. Those who relinquish Christian communion are in a backsliding state; those who backslide are in danger of apostasy. To prevent this latter, the apostle speaks the awful words following. See at the end of this chapter (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.39">Heb 10:39</reference> (note)).
entries.1b0dd3228faec00e63cc32858c843131b31d1ed2: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen53586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53587" type="x-p"/> For if we sin wilfully - If we deliberately, for fear of persecution or from any other motive, renounce the profession of the Gospel and the Author of that Gospel, after having received the knowledge of the truth so as to be convinced that Jesus is the promised Messiah, and that he had sprinkled our hearts from an evil conscience; for such there remaineth no sacrifice for sins; for as the Jewish sacrifices are abolished, as appears by the declaration of God himself in the fortieth Psalm, and Jesus being now the only sacrifice which God will accept, those who reject him have none other; therefore their case must be utterly without remedy. This is the meaning of the apostle, and the case is that of a deliberate apostate - one who has utterly rejected Jesus Christ and his atonement, and renounced the whole Gospel system. It has nothing to do with backsliders in our common use of that term. A man may be overtaken in a fault, or he may deliberately go into sin, and yet neither renounce the Gospel, nor deny the Lord that bought him. His case is dreary and dangerous, but it is not hopeless; no case is hopeless but that of the deliberate apostate, who rejects the whole Gospel system, after having been saved by grace, or convinced of the truth of the Gospel. To him there remaineth no more sacrifice for sin; for there was but the One, Jesus, and this he has utterly rejected.
entries.8a9a59d2f035f34230a628fd78bd3fe0b9064244: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen53587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53588" type="x-p"/> A certain fearful looking for of judgment - From this it is evident that God will pardon no man without a sacrifice for sin; for otherwise, as Dr. Macknight argues, it would not follow, from there remaining to apostates no more sacrifice for sin, that there must remain to them a dreadful expectation of judgment. <div eID="gen53588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53589" type="x-p"/> And fiery indignation - Και πυρος ζηλος· A zeal, or fervor of fire; something similar to the fire that came down from heaven and destroyed Korah and his company; <reference osisRef="Num.16.35">Num 16:35</reference>. <div eID="gen53589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53590" type="x-p"/> Probably the apostle here refers to the case of the unbelieving Jews in general, as in chap. 6 to the dreadful judgment that was coming upon them, and the burning up their temple and city with fire. These people had, by the preaching of Christ and his apostles, received the knowledge of the truth. It was impossible that they could have witnessed his miracles and heard his doctrine without being convinced that he was the Messiah, and that their own system was at an end; but they rejected this only sacrifice at a time when God abolished their own: to that nation, therefore, there remained no other sacrifice for sin; therefore the dreadful judgment came, the fiery indignation was poured out, and they, as adversaries, were devoured by it.
entries.fc6493e211d0117adfb9ce4563ee189f102e4f2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen53590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53591" type="x-p"/> He that despised Moses' law - Αθετησας· He that rejected it, threw it aside, and denied its Divine authority by presumptuous sinning, died without mercy - without any extenuation or mitigation of punishment; <reference osisRef="Num.15.30">Num 15:30</reference>. <div eID="gen53591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53592" type="x-p"/> Under two or three witnesses - That is, when convicted by the testimony of two or three respectable witnesses. See <reference osisRef="Deu.17.6">Deu 17:6</reference>.
entries.b5fa2f61f3b22868cb629180c632e1c121eb6a07: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen53592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53593" type="x-p"/> Of how much sorer punishment - Such offenses were trifling in comparison of this, and in justice the punishment should be proportioned to the offense. <div eID="gen53593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53594" type="x-p"/> Trodden under foot the Son of God - Treated him with the utmost contempt and blasphemy. <div eID="gen53594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53595" type="x-p"/> The blood of the covenant - an unholy thing - The blood of the covenant means here the sacrificial death of Christ, by which the new covenant between God and man was ratified, sealed, and confirmed. And counting this unholy, or common, κοινον, intimates that they expected nothing from it in a sacrificial or atoning way. How near to those persons, and how near to their destruction, do they come in the present day who reject the atoning blood, and say, "that they expect no more benefit from the blood of Christ than they do from that of a cow or a sheep!" Is not this precisely the crime of which the apostle speaks here, and to which he tells us God would show no mercy? <div eID="gen53595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53596" type="x-p"/> Despite unto the Spirit of grace? - Hath insulted the Spirit of grace. The apostle means the Holy Spirit, whose gifts were bestowed in the first age on believers for the confirmation of the Gospel. See <reference osisRef="Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6">Heb 6:4-6</reference>. Wherefore, if one apostatized in the first age, after having been witness to these miraculous gifts, much more after having possessed them himself, he must, like the scribes and Pharisees, have ascribed them to evil spirits; than which a greater indignity could not be done to the Spirit of God. Macknight. This is properly the sin against the Holy Ghost, which has no forgiveness.
entries.a9acaf177235d6a4891ad0d19bdbe8d608c1784b: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen53596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53597" type="x-p"/> Vengeance belongeth unto me - This is the saying of God, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.35">Deu 32:35</reference>, in reference to the idolatrous Gentiles, who were the enemies of his people; and is here with propriety applied to the above apostates, who, being enemies to God's ordinances, and Christ's ministry and merits, must also be enemies to Christ's people; and labor for the destruction of them, and the cause in which they are engaged. <div eID="gen53597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53598" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall judge his people - That is, he shall execute judgment for them; for this is evidently the sense in which the word is used in the place from which the apostle quotes, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.36">Deu 32:36</reference> : For the Lord shall judge his people, and repent himself for his servants, when he seeth that their power is gone. So God will avenge and vindicate the cause of Christianity by destroying its enemies, as he did in the case of the Jewish people, whom he destroyed from being a nation, and made them a proverb of reproach and monuments of his wrathful indignation to the present day.
entries.bf17c6102e4b023e4676a16c20bc6a9a15e48f7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen53598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53599" type="x-p"/> It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God - To fall into the hands of God is to fall under his displeasure; and he who lives for ever can punish for ever. How dreadful to have the displeasure of an eternal, almighty Being to rest on the soul for ever! Apostates, and all the persecutors and enemies of God's cause and people, may expect the heaviest judgments of an incensed Deity: and these, not for a time, but through eternity.
entries.8b1746e6f4f4ad3185243e3306e6979a3c51e9aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen53599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53600" type="x-p"/> But call to remembrance - It appears from this, and indeed from some parts of the Gospel history, that the first believers in Judea were greatly persecuted; our Lord's crucifixion, Stephen's martyrdom, the persecution that arose after the death of Stephen, <reference osisRef="Act.8.1">Act 8:1</reference>, Herod's persecution, <reference osisRef="Act.12.1">Act 12:1</reference>, in which James was killed, and the various persecutions of St. Paul, sufficiently show that this disposition was predominant among that bad people. <div eID="gen53600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53601" type="x-p"/> A great fight of afflictions - Πολλην αθλησιν παθηματων· A great combat or contention of sufferings. Here we have an allusion to the combats at the Grecian games, or to exhibitions of gladiators at the public spectacles; and an intimation how honorable it was to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints, and to overcome through the blood of the Lamb, and their own testimony.
entries.17b04ec2d67115e9c1dbc48b16327778aa3a5130: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen53601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53602" type="x-p"/> Ye were made a gazing-stock - Θεατριζομενοι· Ye were exhibited as wild beasts and other shows at the theatres. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">1Cor 4:9</reference>, where all this is illustrated. <div eID="gen53602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53603" type="x-p"/> Companions of them that were so used - It appears, from <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.14">1Thes 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thes.2.15">1Thes 2:15</reference>, that the Churches of God in Judea were greatly persecuted, and that they believed with courage and constancy in their persecutions. When any victim of persecuting rage was marked out, the rest were prompt to take his part, and acknowledge themselves believers in the same doctrine for which he suffered. This was a noble spirit; many would have slunk into a corner, and put off the marks of Christ, that they might not be exposed to affliction on this account.
entries.c9f443fae14308de22fae35e4a36cf80f63ec394: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen53603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53604" type="x-p"/> Ye had compassion of me in my bonds - Συνεπαθησατε· Ye suffered with me, ye sympathized with me, when bound for the testimony of Jesus. This probably refers to the sympathy they showed towards him, and the help they afforded him, during his long imprisonment in Caesarea and Jerusalem. But instead of τοις δεσμοις μου, my bonds, τοις δεσμιοις, the prisoners, is the reading of AD, and several others, both the Syriac, the Arabic of Erpen, the Coptic, Armenian, Vulgate, some of the Itala, and several of the Greek fathers. This reading appears to be so well supported, that Griesbach has admitted it into the text. If it be genuine, it shows that there had been, and perhaps were then, several bound for the testimony of Jesus, and that the Church in Judea had shown its attachment to Christ by openly acknowledging these prisoners, and ministering to them. <div eID="gen53604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53605" type="x-p"/> Took joyfully the spoiling of your goods - They were deprived of their inheritances, turned out of their houses, and plundered of their goods; they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented. To suffer such persecution patiently was great; to endure it without a murmur was greater; to rejoice in it was greatest of all. But how could they do all this?
